newsitem.title: USA: Semiconductor book-to-bill seen hitting parity.
newsitem.headline: Semiconductor book-to-bill seen hitting parity.

text.p: The Semiconductor Industry Association's widely-watched book-to-bill ratio for the Americas markets in October may top the 1.0 level for the first time this year, industry analysts said.

Estimates for last month's ratio, expected to be released after today's market close, range from 0.99 to 1.03 as recent strong order trends in the personal computer market are expected to have perked up orders, they said.
The book-to-bill ratio measures the value of new orders, or bookings, compared with the value of shipments, or billings.
A book to bill of 1.0 means that for every dollar of computer chips shipped, one dollar of new orders was recorded.

Last month, the preliminary number for September edged up to 0.99, the highest level so far this year and the closed to parity between orders and shipments since the ratio was recorded at 1.12 in December last year.

The year's low point was in March, at 0.79, after personal computer makers had reported disappointing sales in the 1995 Christmas season and memory prices fell amid weaker than anticipated demand and a fresh infusion of added capacity.
But now, with a bullish report last week from Intel Corp, the world's largest semiconductor maker, analysts expect the ratio to have continued to strengthen in October.

"I think you've seen overall semiconductor prices start to firm, especially from the PC side," said Dan Niles, analyst at Robertson, Stephens & Co. in San Francisco, who expects the ratio to come in at 1.03.

"You've started to see bookings really take off for the PC- related semiconductor companies like Intel," he said, noting that Dell Computer Corp's expected quarterly earnings report tomorrow may further confirm the trend.
Intel said last week that it expects its revenues and gross profit margins to be sharply higher in the fourth quarter due to strong demand for personal computer chips.
Shares of Intel were off 1/4 at 122 in mid-afternoon trading, but the stock was still trading firmly, near its all-time trading high of last week of 124-3/4.

The quarterly book-to-bill ratio for the Americas is the most widely-monitored figure, although industry executives and analysts have long faulted it for being unrepresentative of an industry which has become global in nature.

To address the issue, SIA members have sponsored a project to develop a worldwide number, although it is a challenge to get up-to-date data from far-flung regions and data collection generally lags the Americas figure by a month.

Last month, the industry group said the World Semiconductor Trade Statistics program, which collects the numbers, reported the August Worldwide figure for Japan, Asia, Europe and the Americas combined was 0.97 percent.
